body.heading: Clutter is a queue of small decisions
paragraphs: Every object on your desk is silently asking a question: file me, answer me, finish me, throw me away. You may ignore the questions, but part of your attention keeps hearing them, and it shows up as a vague reluctance to start.
A clear desk does not make you a better person. It simply lowers the number of things competing with the one thing you chose.

body.heading: The two-minute reset
paragraphs: Before a focused session, set a timer for two minutes and move everything unrelated to this task out of sight: into a drawer, a box, a pile behind you. Not sorted, not dealt with — just gone from view. Sorting is a different job for a different time.
Leave only what the task needs: the document, the notebook, water, perhaps the later list. When the timer ends, begin. The reset is a doorway ritual, and its sameness is what makes it work.

body.heading: A landing strip for afterwards
paragraphs: Things will land on the desk during the day; that is what desks are for. The reset is not about keeping the desk empty forever. It is about starting each session from clear rather than from cluttered.

If a full reset feels impossible in a shared or busy space, shrink it: clear one square — the space directly in front of you, roughly the size of a placemat. Attention mostly lives in that square anyway.

takeaway: Two minutes of clearing buys a calmer start; the desk serves the task, not the reverse.
